title: Crafting Your App Idea with Reddit: How to Research What Players Want
summary: Use Reddit to find what players ask for before you build. Search threads, note patterns, ask good questions, and turn it all into one game idea.
body_markdown:
Reddit is one of the easiest places to hear what players say about games in their own words. Before you build anything, you can spend a few hours reading threads, write down what people keep asking for, and turn those notes into one clear game idea. This guide covers that research step, how to do it without spamming anyone, and what to do with your notes once you have them.


## Why research a game idea on Reddit first


Players post their wishes and complaints without being asked. Someone asks for "a game like X, but shorter." Old threads stay up and are searchable, so you can read years of conversation about a genre in an afternoon.


Keep one caution in mind. Reddit is a sample of players, and the loudest voices aren't always the biggest group. Treat what you find as a starting point to test, then check it with a prototype.


## Step 1: Find the right subreddits


Start broad, then narrow down.


- **r/gamedev** is where developers talk about design, scope, and finishing games. It's useful for seeing what other creators struggle with.
- **r/indiegaming** mixes players and developers sharing indie games. It shows you what catches players' attention.
- **r/iPad** is full of iPad owners. If you plan to make a game for iPad, this is where you learn what those players use their device for.


Then look for communities about the genre you care about. Use Reddit's search for the genre name ("cozy farming games," "roguelike," "puzzle games") and check which communities come up.


Before you spend time in one, check for recent posts with real comment threads.


## Step 2: Read the rules before you post anything


Every subreddit sets its own rules, usually in the sidebar or the About tab. Read them first. Many communities ban self-promotion, limit how often you can post about your own work, or ask you to use a weekly feedback thread instead.


A good habit is to read a community for a week before you post. You learn the tone, what gets removed, and which questions come up often. Posts that break the rules get removed, and repeat problems can get you banned.


## Step 3: Search for recurring complaints and requests


This is where most of the useful material shows up. Search inside a subreddit for phrases like these:


- "I wish there was a game"
- "looking for a game like"
- "why are there no"
- "games that don't have"
- "recommend a game for"


Sort by Top and set the time range to the past year. Then read the comments. They often add the detail you need, like "something I can play in five minutes on the train."


## Step 4: Write down patterns, not single posts


One post is an anecdote. The same request showing up across many threads is a pattern. Keep a simple note with four columns:


1. What people want (or dislike)
2. How many times you saw it
3. A short quote in the player's own words
4. A link to the thread


Say you read 30 threads and see eight people ask for puzzle games with short levels and no timers. That's worth more than one viral post with a big idea. Patterns also show you what players already dislike, so you know what to leave out.


## Step 5: Ask good questions without spamming


Sometimes reading isn't enough and you want to ask. Check the rules again, then ask one specific question.


A good question is easy to answer and shows you've done some reading: "For short puzzle games on iPad, do you prefer levels you can finish in two minutes or longer sessions?"


A weak question asks for attention: "Would you play my game? Here's the link."


A few ground rules:


- Say you're a developer researching an idea. People are more helpful when you're open about it.
- Post in one community at a time. Copying the same question into many subreddits at once reads as spam.
- Reply to the people who answer you, and thank them.
- Never buy upvotes, use extra accounts, or ask friends to vote or comment. Fake engagement breaks Reddit's rules, and it ruins the data you came for.


When you later want feedback on a playable build,[this guide to writing a Reddit post for indie devs](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/reddit-post-for-indie-devs) covers how to frame that kind of post.


## Step 6: Turn your notes into one game idea sentence


Pick the strongest pattern from your notes and write one sentence:


"A \[genre\] game for \[players\] where you \[core action\], so \[the thing they said they wanted\]."


For example: "A puzzle game for iPad players who commute, where you slide tiles to connect paths, so each level takes about two minutes and needs no timer."


If the sentence gets long, the idea is too big. Cut it down until the core action is clear. For a sense of how small a first idea can be, look at these[8 small game ideas to prototype on iPad](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/8-easy-game-ideas-you-can-create-in-under-an-hour-on-ipad) .


## Next step: build a prototype


Reddit tells you what players say. A prototype tells you what they actually do. Once you have your sentence, build the smallest playable version of it in hyperPad on iPad. You connect Behaviors (actions and events) into a flowchart of your game's logic, so you can test the core action without writing traditional code.[Rapid prototyping games on iPad](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/rapid-prototyping-games-on-ipad) walks through how to keep that first build small and fast.


Later, the communities you studied can become part of your launch plan too.[This mobile game marketing strategy for solo developers](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/how-to-market-your-mobile-game) covers what to do when your game is ready for players.


## FAQ


### Is it okay to promote my game on Reddit?


Only where a subreddit's rules allow it. Many communities have a weekly thread or a flair for sharing your own work. Use those, and keep the post focused on what you want to learn from players.


### How long should I spend researching?


A few hours spread over a week is usually enough to spot patterns. If you keep seeing the same requests, stop reading and start building.


### What if no one is asking for my idea?


You can still build it. Silence may mean the idea is new, or that the players who'd want it hang out somewhere else. A small prototype is the fastest way to find out.


Take your one-sentence idea and build it as a single playable Scene this week. Then follow[how to validate a game idea with a playable iPad prototype](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog/app-idea-with-reddit) to test it with real players.
